[[File:Helen Abbott Merrill with Students.jpg|alt=A group of white women posed around a desk and in front of a chalkboard|thumb|Helen Abbott Merrill with math students at Wellesley College]]
'''Helen Abbot Merrill''' (March 30, 1864 &ndash;  May 1, 1949) was an American mathematician, educator and textbook author. She was chair of the [[mathematics]] department at [[Wellesley College]], where she taught from 1893 to 1932.

==Early life and education==
Merrill was born on March 30, 1864, in [[Llewellyn Park, New Jersey]].<ref name="asc">{{citation|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/hmerrill.htm|title=Helen Abbot Merrill|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|publisher=Agnes Scott College|date=February 25, 2016|first=Larry|last=Riddle|access-date=March 26, 2020|archive-date=March 28, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170328094411/https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/hmerrill.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Her father George Merrill was a [[New Jersey]] insurance claims adjustor; her mother was Emily Dodge Abbot Merrill. She lived in [[Newburyport, Massachusetts]], for some of her childhood.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=May 3, 1949 |title=Helen A. Merrill, Headed Math Department at Wellesley College, 1916 to 1932 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-daily-globe-helen-a-merrill/174598815/ |access-date=June 16, 2025 |work=The Boston Daily Globe |pages=13 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> She entered Wellesley College in 1882; she intended to major in Greek and Latin, but switched to mathematics after one year, and graduated in 1886.<ref name="asc" /> She pursued further studies at the [[University of Chicago]] and in Germany.<ref name=":0" /> In 1903 she earned a PhD in mathematics at [[Yale University]] under the direction of [[James Pierpont (mathematician)|James Pierpont]]. Her thesis was "On Solutions of Differential Equations which possess an Oscillation Theorem."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Merrill |first=Helen A. |date=1903 |title=On Solutions of Differential Equations Which Possess an Oscillatoin Theorem |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1986411 |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=423–433 |doi=10.2307/1986411 |jstor=1986411 |issn=0002-9947|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Her younger brother [[William P. Merrill]] was a noted Presbyterian minister, hymn writer, and pacifist.<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Pierson Merrill |url=https://centuryarchives.org/member-directory/?PersonID=1968 |access-date=June 16, 2025 |website=Member Directory, Century Archives |archive-date=January 21, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121153636/https://centuryarchives.org/member-directory/?PersonID=1968 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Career ==
Merrill taught at girls' schools in New York and Pennsylvania after college.<ref name=":0" /> She taught mathematics at Wellesley College beginning in 1893, and she was chair of the mathematics department from 1916 to 1932.<ref name=":0" /><ref>Wellesley College, ''[https://repository.wellesley.edu/object/wellesley641 The Legenda]'' (1929 yearbook).</ref> She rebuilt Wellesley's collection of cardboard mathematical models, after a fire destroyed the original set.<ref name=":1" /> Upon her retirement in 1932 from Wellesley, she was given the title [[professor emerita]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=June 18, 1932 |title=Three Retiring as Professors Served Wellesley 100 Years |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-daily-globe-three-retiring-as/174597421/ |access-date=June 16, 2025 |work=The Boston Daily Globe |pages=2 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

She became a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1911.<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 3, 1911 |title=Men of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/boston-evening-transcript-men-of-arts-an/174597295/ |access-date=June 16, 2025 |work=Boston Evening Transcript |pages=9 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 1920 she was appointed vice-president of the [[Mathematical Association of America]].<ref>Henrion, C. "Helen Abbot Merrill" in ''Women of Mathematics: A Bibliographic Sourcebook'', L. Grinstein, P. Campbell, eds. New York: Greenwood Press (1987): 147–151.</ref>

== Publications ==
Merrill wrote two textbooks with her Wellesley colleague [[Clara Eliza Smith]]: ''Selected Topics in Higher Algebra'' (Norwood, 1914) and ''A First Course in Higher Algebra'' (Macmillan, 1917).<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/smith.htm|title=Clara Eliza Smith|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|first=Larry|last=Riddle|publisher=Agnes Scott College|date=February 25, 2016|access-date=May 8, 2018|archive-date=March 29, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170329024133/https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/smith.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>Reviews of ''A First Course in Higher Algebra'':
*{{citation|title=none|journal=The Journal of Education|volume=87|issue=2|date=January 1918|page=49|jstor=42826577}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=Mary E.|last=Wells|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=25|issue=2|date=February 1918|pages=72–74|doi=10.2307/2971993|jstor=2971993|hdl=2027/uc2.ark:/13960/t2794577q|hdl-access=free}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=Philip E. B.|last=Jourdain|journal=Science Progress|volume=12|issue=48|date=April 1918|page=684|jstor=43426456}}
</ref> She also wrote a book titled ''[[Mathematical Excursions]]'' in 1933, meant to explain some mathematical concepts to a young audience.<ref>Reviews of ''Mathematical Excursions'':
*{{citation|title=none|journal=The Mathematics Teacher|volume=26|issue=5|date=May 1933|page=315|jstor=27951594}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=Mary E.|last=Wells|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=40|issue=10|date=December 1933|pages=602–603|doi=10.2307/2301690|jstor=2301690}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=David Eugene|last=Smith|author-link=David Eugene Smith|journal=The Mathematics Teacher|volume=26|issue=8|date=December 1933|pages=499–501|jstor=27951644}}
*{{citation|title=none|author=P. W. L. C.|journal=Junior-Senior High School Clearing House|volume=8|issue=5|department=The Marginal Fifty per Cent|date=January 1934|page=319|jstor=30174218}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=Alex|last=Inglis|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|volume=19|issue=232|date=February 1935|page=62|doi=10.2307/3606651|jstor=3606651}}
*{{citation|title=none|first=Samuel L.|last=Greitzer|author-link=Samuel L. Greitzer|journal=The Mathematics Teacher|volume=51|issue=6|date=October 1958|page=481|jstor=27955732}}
*{{citation|title=none|journal=zbMATH|first=R.|last=Sprague|author-link=Roland Sprague|zbl=0080.00105}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Merrill died in 1949, at the age of 85, in [[Wellesley, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 3, 1949 |title=Obituary for Helen A. Merrill |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-star-ledger-obituary-for-helen-a-me/174598098/ |access-date=June 16, 2025 |work=The Star-Ledger |pages=18 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
